tagline: Chasing light through the streets of Delhi
aboutText:
I picked up my first camera at seventeen — a second-hand Canon my father bought from Palika Bazaar. That summer I walked through Chandni Chowk every morning before the heat set in, photographing chai-wallahs, cycle-rickshaws, and the way sunlight cut through the gaps between old havelis. Ten years later, those lanes still pull me back.

Today I split my time between documentary street work and portrait commissions. My goal is simple: find the extraordinary in the everyday. Whether it's a Holi celebration exploding with colour or a quiet moment between two strangers on the Metro, I want my photos to make you pause and feel something real.

quote: Keshav has this rare ability to make you forget the camera is there. Our engagement photos feel like stolen moments — natural, warm, and full of emotion. Every time we look at them, we're right back in that golden-hour light at Lodhi Garden.

I hired Keshav for a two-week Rajasthan trip to document my solo travel journal. He has an incredible eye for detail — the way he captured the textures of Jaisalmer's sandstone and the chaos of Pushkar's camel fair was absolutely magical. I've printed six of his shots as large canvases for my living room.

Working with Keshav on my NGO's annual report was an absolute pleasure. He spent three days in the field with our team and came back with images that told our story better than any words could. His patience and respect for the people he photographs really sets him apart.

title: Why I Still Shoot on the Streets of Old Delhi
excerpt: Old Delhi is not a pretty city. It is loud, chaotic, and overwhelming. But after ten years of walking its lanes, I still find something new every single morning.

children.text: Old Delhi is not a pretty city. It is loud, chaotic, and relentlessly overwhelming. The first time I walked through Chandni Chowk with a camera, I was eighteen and terrified of bumping into people. A decade later, those same lanes feel like home.

Between 6 and 7 in the morning, before the shutters roll up and the traffic takes over, there is this perfect window of light. It cuts diagonally through the narrow alleys and turns ordinary walls into gold. That one hour is worth the entire day.

I have tried photographing other cities the same way — Varanasi, Jaipur, Kolkata — and each has its own rhythm. But Old Delhi's rhythm is the one I know by heart. The chai-wallah at the corner of Dariba Kalan who waves me over every Tuesday. The paper-kite maker whose hands move so fast they blur at 1/250th of a second. These are not just subjects; they are neighbours.
What Street Photography Means to Me

Street photography is not about stealing moments from strangers. It is about being present — fully, completely present — in a place and letting the frame compose itself. Some days I come home with three hundred exposures and keep two. Other days a single image stops me in my tracks and I know the walk was worth it.

title: Five Lessons from Photographing Holi in Mathura
excerpt: Holi in Mathura is pure sensory overload. Here is what I have learned across four years of covering the festival — and the mistakes I keep making.

children.text: Holi in Mathura is nothing like Holi anywhere else. The colours are thicker, the crowd is denser, and the energy is turned up to eleven. I have covered the festival four times now, and every year I learn something new — usually the hard way.

My first year, I wrapped my camera in a plastic bag and thought that was enough. It was not. Gulaal powder found its way into the lens mount within twenty minutes. Now I use a proper rain cover, a UV filter I do not mind sacrificing, and I keep my bag zipped at all times. If you are bringing a second body, leave it in a sealed dry-bag until you need it.

The best light — and the best portraits — happen before the main event starts. People are still getting ready, applying colour to each other gently, laughing quietly. Once the DJ truck arrives and the crowd surges, you are in pure survival mode. Get your slow, contemplative shots in early.

You will get drenched. Your clothes will be ruined. Your face will be every colour of the rainbow. That is the entire point. The best photos happen when you stop trying to stay clean and start participating. People open up to you when they see you are not hiding behind your camera — you are part of the celebration.
